The Brazilian flathead (Percophis brasiliensis) reaches an ultimate total length of 68.5 centimeters [Li = 68.5 centimeters], making it one of the larger benthic predators inhabiting the coastal waters of the southwestern Atlantic. Field surveys along the continental shelf off southern Brazil have documented that females typically attain a greater asymptotic size than males, a pattern commonly observed in sexually dimorphic teleosts with indeterminate growth. The species demonstrates a relatively slow growth rate during its juvenile phase, which likely reflects the energetic demands of occupying a demersal habitat where prey availability fluctuates seasonally. Age determination based on otolith readings from specimens collected over a five-year period has provided valuable insights into the species' growth trajectory. The maximum recorded adult body mass associated with this length is approximately 1.82 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 1.82 kilograms], though individuals exceeding this threshold are rarely encountered in commercial trawl catches. This substantial size indicates that Percophis brasiliensis occupies a high trophic position within its ecosystem, preying primarily on small demersal fishes and cephalopods. Comparative analyses with related members of the Percophidae family reveal that this species exhibits one of the highest reported values for maximum length within the genus. This extended discussion helps contextualize the species' morphological and ecological attributes.

The age at birth for Percophis brasiliensis has been estimated at 9.5 days [ab = 9.5 days] when the incubating eggs are maintained at a stable temperature of 10.4 °C [T = 10.4 °C], which closely mirrors the thermal conditions recorded in the species' primary spawning grounds during the austral winter. This relatively brief embryonic period, derived from observations on the embryogenesis of a related notothenioid, reflects the rapid developmental rate characteristic of pelagic eggs spawned in temperate waters. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae exhibit a remarkably low wet weight at birth of only 0.000524 grams [Wwb = 0.000524 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter of approximately 1 millimeter typical of this species. The larval phase is characterized by a substantial yolk reserve that sustains the endotrophic larva through the critical period before mouth opening and first exogenous feeding. The timing of eclosion is tightly linked to water temperature, and deviations from this optimal thermal regime could delay hatching and reduce larval survival rates in the wild. These early life-history traits have important implications for recruitment variability.

The age at which individuals attain sexual maturity differs notably between the sexes in Percophis brasiliensis, with females reaching puberty at a considerably larger size than males. The total length at puberty for female specimens has been recorded at 38.71 centimeters [Lp = 38.71 centimeters], and the corresponding wet weight at this developmental milestone is approximately 311 grams [Wwp = approximately 311 grams], a body mass that reflects the energetic investment required for gonadal maturation and the onset of vitellogenesis. In contrast, male individuals achieve sexual maturity at a smaller total length of 29.24 centimeters [Lp = 29.24 centimeters], a disparity that likely arises from differences in the energetic costs associated with gamete production between the two sexes. The earlier maturation of males may confer a reproductive advantage by allowing them to participate in multiple spawning events earlier in the breeding season. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from captured specimens has confirmed that both sexes exhibit group-synchronous oocyte development, a pattern indicative of multiple-batch spawning behavior during the reproductive period. This reproductive strategy is commonly observed among demersal fishes inhabiting temperate continental shelves.

The lifespan of Percophis brasiliensis has been estimated to extend up to 19 years [am = up to 19 years] under the prevailing thermal conditions of 10.4 °C [T = 10.4 °C], which corresponds to the mean annual temperature recorded in its primary habitat on the continental shelf. This longevity is relatively substantial for a percophid of its size and suggests that the species follows a comparatively slow pace of life, with delayed senescence and extended reproductive output over the adult years. Mark-recapture studies conducted along the coast of Rio Grande do Sul have corroborated this maximum age estimate, with recaptured individuals showing consistent otolith growth increments that align with the predicted lifespan. The combination of a large ultimate body size, prolonged lifespan, and relatively late reproductive maturation positions Percophis brasiliensis as a K-selected strategist among the demersal fish community. This life-history configuration makes the species particularly susceptible to overfishing, as removal of older, larger individuals can rapidly erode the spawning stock biomass and compromise population resilience. These demographic characteristics underscore the need for careful fisheries management.

Reproductive output in Percophis brasiliensis has been quantified through examination of gravid females captured during the peak spawning season, which extends from June through September. Counts of hydrated oocytes from mature ovaries indicate that each female produces approximately 250,000 to 350,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 250,000 to 350,000 eggs per spawning event], with individuals typically completing two to three such events over the course of a single breeding season [F_R_i = two to three such events over the course of a single breeding season]. The small, buoyant eggs, each measuring roughly 1 millimeter in diameter, are released into the pelagic environment where they undergo rapid development influenced by ambient temperature. The production of such a large number of small offspring is consistent with an r-selected reproductive strategy at the gamete level, even though the species as a whole exhibits K-selected adult life-history traits. Fecundity increases proportionally with female body size, so the largest individuals make a disproportionately large contribution to annual recruitment. This batch-spawning mode ensures that at least some larvae encounter favorable feeding conditions during the extended spawning period. Overall, these life-history parameters provide a comprehensive basis for understanding population dynamics.
